strengths: Soundness/significance: MARS-SQL presents a coherent three-stage system—schema grounding, interactive SQL generation, and learned validation—and evaluates it on BIRD-dev, Spider-test, and Spider-DK. The reported execution accuracies are strong: 77.84%, 89.75%, and 78.13%, respectively.

The component studies are useful. Table 3 compares grounding and selection variants; Table 10 varies training and inference turn limits; Table 11 reports the Best-of-N ceiling; and Table 14 compares the verifier with self-consistency and LLM judges. These results generally support the value of interaction and learned candidate selection.

The interactive generator is practically motivated: database errors and query results provide actionable feedback, and the worked example clearly illustrates recovery from a misspelled table and an incorrect filter.
Presentation is generally organized, with formal definitions, prompts, dataset descriptions, training hyperparameters, and separate reproducibility and ethics statements.
The paper acknowledges deployment risk from incorrect queries and recommends human oversight. The benchmark data are public and the stated experiments do not raise major ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: Essential experimental details are missing or ambiguous. The paper does not clearly specify the exact inference configuration producing Table 2, including the number of candidates, interaction limit, verifier rounds, decoding parameters, or total execution budget. Different appendices use 5 or 10 turns and up to 8, 16, or 32 candidates, making the headline results difficult to interpret or compare fairly.

The comparisons do not control for inference-time computation or database interactions. MARS-SQL samples multiple multi-turn trajectories and reranks them, while many baselines may use substantially smaller budgets. Consequently, the claimed state of the art does not isolate methodological improvement from test-time scaling.

No repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are provided. This is especially important for RL training and stochastic Best-of-N generation. Several cross-benchmark gains are small—for example, the full system improves over the no-grounder variant by only 0.56 points on Spider and 1.12 points on Spider-DK—so the claim that every agent is indispensable is overstated.

The ablations are not sufficiently controlled. “Generator Only (Base),” “w/o verifier,” and “w/o Grounder” change multiple aspects of training, grounding, sampling, or selection, and the caption mentions SFT versus RL although no corresponding controlled SFT generator result appears. The claimed synergistic effect therefore lacks a clean factorial comparison.

The verifier methodology is underspecified and internally inconsistent. Section 3.3 says it scores full trajectories over M stochastic reasoning rounds, whereas Table 12 appears to provide only a proposed solution and asks for a Yes/No judgment; M and the construction of its averaged probability are not reported. It is also unclear whether the verifier receives the complete schema and execution observations. Without these inputs, logical SQL verification is generally impossible.

Verifier labels are based on execution equality on a single database instance, which can mark semantically incorrect SQL as positive. The manuscript neither analyzes this label noise nor evaluates semantic robustness on alternative database contents. Execution accuracy alone also does not substantiate broader claims of reliability or real-world robustness.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Multi-stage Text-to-SQL pipelines, ReAct-style database interaction, execution-reward RL, Best-of-N sampling, and generative verifiers all have close precedents; the manuscript does not sharply distinguish its technical contribution from cited systems such as SkyRL-SQL, CHASE-SQL, and prior generative-verifier work.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance in its current form. The abstract says code is available but gives no URL, while the reproducibility statement only promises release upon publication. Important GRPO settings such as group size, clipping and KL coefficients, training duration, sequence limits, hardware count, random seeds, and total compute are absent.

Presentation requires substantial polishing: there are broken or incorrect appendix references, malformed equations, typographical errors, inconsistent terminology, and visibly invalid SQL in examples due to missing identifier quoting and curly quotation marks. Table 1 also makes sweeping open-source/closed-source capability claims without a defensible survey basis.

The limitations and ethics discussion is too narrow. It does not address privacy and authorization risks of sending schema or values to models, potentially expensive or unsafe database execution, dialect portability, read-only sandboxing, or the gap between benchmark databases and enterprise deployment. These omissions do not create an immediate ethical violation, but weaken the deployment claims.

strengths: The three-stage decomposition into schema grounding, interactive generation, and candidate validation is clearly motivated and easy to understand. The Think-Act-Observe interface is appropriate for Text-to-SQL because database errors and execution results can provide useful corrective feedback.

The reported results are strong: 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev, 89.75% on Spider-test, and 78.13% on Spider-DK. The paper evaluates both in-domain and out-of-domain settings and includes component, interaction-turn, grounding, candidate-count, and selection-method studies.

The grounding results and Pass@N analysis provide useful evidence that schema pruning and diverse trajectory generation can improve the candidate pool. Prompts, dataset sizes, and some training hyperparameters are included in the appendix.

The paper acknowledges the risk of incorrect generated queries, recommends human oversight in critical applications, and states that the experiments use established public benchmarks without sensitive user data.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central claim that environmental interaction produces robust self-correction is not adequately isolated. Increasing the number of turns simultaneously changes training, inference compute, and opportunities to resample SQL. There is no controlled comparison against equal-compute non-interactive refinement, feedback-free multi-turn reasoning, or one-shot generation with the same token/query budget. A single qualitative correction example cannot establish the claimed mechanism.

Soundness: the Validation Agent is technically underspecified and partly incoherent. Equation 5 averages the probability of the Yes token over M stochastic reasoning rounds, but the supplied prompt requires Yes or No as the first token; repeated forward evaluations of that token under the same conditioning are not stochastic unless an additional procedure is used, and none is described. The prompt also omits an explicit database schema despite the text claiming evaluation against the full schema and context.

Soundness and presentation: important definitions are incomplete or inconsistent. The grounding reward does not specify the case where the prediction is N and the gold label is Y. M is used both for trajectory turns and validation rounds, and the generation objective alternates between RGen(T) and RGen(tau). The reported Spider selection rate of 97.15% is also difficult to reconcile with Table 14's 89.75 selected accuracy and 90.68 Pass@8 upper bound, whose ratio is approximately 98.97%.

The ablations do not cleanly attribute gains. The Generator Only row is labeled Base, whereas other rows combine RL training, grounding, and verification; thus the claimed synergy and indispensability of every agent are confounded by training strategy and inference budget. On Spider, removing the grounder changes accuracy only from 89.75% to 89.19%, which does not support a broad claim that every component is indispensable.

Significance and originality are limited relative to the framing. Schema linking followed by generation and reranking is an established Text-to-SQL pipeline; ReAct-style database interaction, execution-reward RL, Best-of-N sampling, and next-token generative verification are all adapted from prior work. Their integration may be useful, but the paper does not demonstrate a sufficiently new algorithmic principle or new understanding of interactive reasoning.

The state-of-the-art comparison is not sufficiently controlled. Systems differ in model size, training data, access to Spider data, interaction capabilities, candidate counts, and test-time compute, yet efficiency, latency, token usage, database executions, and hardware cost are not reported. There are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests, making small differences such as 89.75% versus 89.65% unconvincing as evidence of superiority.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the central RL result. The abstract's code-availability statement contains no link, while the reproducibility statement only promises release after publication. Missing details include GPU count and training time, optimizer settings, GRPO group size G, clipping and KL coefficients, number of updates or epochs, maximum sequence lengths, checkpoint-selection procedure, random seeds, exact execution sandbox, and complete evaluation commands.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. Table 1 makes unsupported categorical claims that open-source frameworks lack multi-agent architecture or complex-schema support, contradicting the paper's own related work and baseline taxonomy. Numerous typographical and notation errors further impede confidence in the technical account.

The ethics discussion addresses erroneous answers but overlooks operational risks introduced by live database interaction, including mutating or expensive SQL, access-control violations, leakage through observations, and safeguards needed for deployment. The generation prompt does not explicitly restrict actions to read-only queries, and there is no dedicated limitations discussion covering benchmark contamination, execution-accuracy weaknesses, or deployment validity.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical results are strong across complementary settings: 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev, 89.75% on Spider-test, and 78.13% on Spider-DK. The Spider evaluations provide useful evidence of cross-schema transfer because training uses only BIRD.

Soundness: The paper includes substantial ablation evidence covering schema grounding, RL versus base generation, interaction-turn budgets, candidate-pool size, and several selection methods. Particularly informative are the grounder recall/precision results and the separation of greedy, Pass@8, and selected accuracy.

Significance: A fully trained, modular Text-to-SQL pipeline based on 7B models is practically useful. The large gains over the reported generator-only configuration and competitive results against substantially larger or proprietary systems make the approach relevant to the community.

Originality: Although the ingredients are established, combining RL-trained schema grounding, multi-turn execution-grounded generation, and a learned generative verifier into one coherent system is a useful systems contribution. Training the interaction policy rather than relying solely on prompted self-correction is the most interesting aspect.
Presentation: The three-stage architecture is easy to understand, and the prompts, qualitative interaction example, and extensive appendix make the overall workflow relatively transparent.

Ethics: The manuscript explicitly discusses incorrect-query risks, human oversight, benchmark data privacy, and its use of LLM assistance. No material ethical concern arises from the benchmark experiments themselves.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet adequate for the headline results. The abstract's code URL is blank, while the reproducibility statement only promises release after publication. Essential details are missing, including RL epochs or update counts, group size, KL coefficient, clipping parameters, GPU count and total compute, random seeds, checkpoint selection, and an unambiguous specification of the candidate and interaction budgets used for every main-table result.

The method specification contains consequential ambiguities. The grounding reward has no stated case for predicting an irrelevant table when the ground truth is relevant. For validation, Equation 5 averages the probability of "Yes" over stochastic reasoning rounds even though the model is described as producing a single-token decision; it is unclear what is sampled or why repeated next-token probabilities differ. The symbol M is also used for both interaction turns and validation rounds.

The verifier description is internally inconsistent. Section 3 says it receives complete trajectories, Appendix H says it evaluates against the full schema and context, but the displayed verifier prompt contains only the question, external knowledge, and an unspecified solution_text field. It does not explicitly include the schema or execution observations. This matters because many SQL errors cannot be judged without schema and database context.

The state-of-the-art and robustness claims are stronger than the evidence supports. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests are reported; the claimed Spider advantage over XiYan-SQL is only 0.10 percentage points. Baselines also have heterogeneous training data, model access, prompting, and inference budgets. Reporting MARS-SQL simply as "7B" obscures that the deployed pipeline contains three separately trained 7B agents and multiple rollouts.

Execution accuracy on a single database instance can reward semantically incorrect queries that happen to return the same result. The paper provides no test-suite accuracy, manual error analysis, or breakdown by query difficulty, so claims of semantic correctness, reliability, and robust self-correction remain only partially supported.

Originality is moderate rather than high: multi-turn execution-based RL is already represented by the cited SkyRL-SQL work, while schema pruning, best-of-N generation, and generative verification are established ideas. The manuscript should isolate more clearly what differs algorithmically from these closest predecessors rather than primarily emphasizing their integration.

The claimed efficient selection and practical dependability are not evaluated in systems terms. Eight trajectories with up to five or ten database interactions, followed by a separate verifier, may be expensive; latency, query count, memory, and total inference cost are absent. Evaluation is also limited to SQLite-style academic benchmarks rather than the enterprise setting invoked in the motivation.

The ethics discussion is welcome but incomplete for deployment: an interactive agent executing model-generated SQL should be evaluated under read-only permissions, sandboxing, resource limits, and defenses against sensitive-data exposure or destructive queries. The manuscript also lacks a dedicated limitations discussion covering these risks and the method's benchmark and dialect dependence.

strengths: Soundness: The paper reports strong execution accuracy on several benchmarks, including 77.84% on BIRD-dev, 89.75% on Spider-test, and 78.13% on Spider-DK. It also includes component ablations, best-of-N analysis, interaction-turn studies, and grounding precision/recall measurements.

Significance: Training an SQL agent to use live execution feedback for iterative correction is practically relevant. The qualitative examples clearly illustrate recovery from schema errors, incorrect filters, and pagination mistakes.

Presentation: The three-stage grounding-generation-validation workflow is easy to understand, and the manuscript provides extensive appendices covering prompts, hyperparameters, latency, token consumption, memory, and training cost.

The efficiency discussion is unusually thorough: it reports the approximately 21B total parameter footprint, sequential and resident-memory scenarios, several cost-accuracy operating points, and matched-latency baselines.
The paper acknowledges an important limitation of its approach: although each agent is 7B-scale, the complete system is more expensive than a single 7B model.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central causal evidence is not reliable. Table 23 describes each mechanism as an isolated addition beyond the same 62.78% baseline, yet adds the three gains—56, 44, and 131 solved cases—without accounting for overlapping successes, obtaining exactly the full system's 231 cases. If these are sequential additions, they are order-dependent rather than isolated effects; if they are independent additions, they cannot generally be summed. The evaluated configurations and candidate sets needed to interpret this analysis are not specified.

The validation procedure is internally inconsistent. Equation 4 averages the probability of the first 'Yes' token over M stochastic validation rounds, while Table 30 requires 'Yes' or 'No' to be the first output. For a fixed model and identical context, that next-token probability is deterministic; sampling later tokens cannot change it. The claimed benefit and substantial cost of eight validation samples therefore lack a clear technical explanation.

The principal ablation does not cleanly separate RL, interactivity, grounding, sampling, and verification. For example, Table 2 changes multiple elements between rows, while the strict baseline is variously reported as 62.78%, 66.37%, and 69.30% under insufficiently distinguished configurations. The approximately eight-point gain from adding grounding to the RL-generator-plus-verifier row also conflicts with the smaller isolated grounding gain without an interaction analysis.

The state-of-the-art comparison mixes systems with different training data, preprocessing, external knowledge, model access, and inference budgets. The later latency controls are useful but cover only a few baselines and do not resolve the comparability of the headline table. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests are supplied, despite stochastic RL and sampling.

Originality: The claim that this is the first interactive RL approach for tool-augmented Text-to-SQL is insufficiently supported. The manuscript itself cites SkyRL-SQL as a multi-turn RL system and other closely related agentic/RL Text-to-SQL methods, but provides neither a precise conceptual distinction nor a direct comparison against SkyRL-SQL. Grounding, ReAct-style execution, GRPO, best-of-N generation, and generative verification are individually established ideas, making the originality primarily their combination.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims. The abstract ends with an empty 'Code is available at' statement. Important details are inconsistent or missing: the text states batch size 64 while Table 4 reports 128; the claimed 35k training examples are not reconciled with 90,102 grounding instances, about 16,000 verifier instances, and generator data; convergence curves and random seeds are absent; and several inference settings vary across sections.

Some numerical and reporting inconsistencies further weaken confidence. The GPT-5 Spider-test score is 78.39 in Table 1 but 77.10 in Table 7; the reported stage latencies sum to 22.13 rather than 22.12 seconds; and projected system-optimized latency and claims that SFT would require 15 million examples and 3–4 months are estimates rather than measured evidence.

The verifier-training description is ambiguous: for questions with no correct sampled trajectory, the gold SQL is inserted as a suggestion, but the exact constructed input, label, and safeguards against shortcut learning are not explained. It is also unclear how the verifier can assess database-specific semantics because its displayed prompt contains no database schema or execution observation.

Limitations and ethics are incomplete. The discussion focuses almost exclusively on compute. An agent allowed to execute generated SQL against a live database raises concerns about read-only enforcement, destructive queries, access control, prompt injection through database content, sensitive-data exposure, and misleading but executable results. The impact statement is largely aspirational and does not state concrete safeguards.

strengths: Significance: Improving reliable Text-to-SQL generation is practically important, and the proposed combination of schema grounding, interactive generation, and candidate validation is potentially useful.
Empirical scope: The paper reports results on BIRD, Spider, Spider-DK, and SParC, along with component ablations, turn-budget studies, best-of-N analyses, and latency/token/VRAM measurements.
Reported performance is strong: MARS-SQL reaches 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test, exceeding the baselines listed in the main table.

Presentation: The three-stage workflow is easy to understand, and the main architecture figures and most tables communicate the intended system clearly. The paper also honestly acknowledges that the deployed system has three 7B agents, an approximately 21B-parameter footprint, and greater inference cost than a single 7B model.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central attribution claims are not established by controlled experiments. The paper compares systems with different training data, parameter counts, sampling budgets, and inference procedures. Table 3 then labels gains from separately evaluated mechanisms as additive and sums them to the full-system improvement, although this does not isolate interactions or constitute a causal decomposition. The largest reported isolated gain is from reranking (+8.54 points), while interactive RL contributes only +2.89 points, weakening the paper's emphasis on interactive policy learning as the main explanation.

Experimental configurations are internally inconsistent. The BIRD baseline is variously reported as 54.43/54.56, 62.78, and 66.37 without an adequate mapping between configurations. The text states a batch size of 64, Table 4 states 128, and Table 8 again states 64. The Spider GPT-5 result is 78.39 in Table 1 but 77.10 in Table 7. These discrepancies materially reduce confidence in the reported comparisons.

The validator description is not reproducible or internally coherent. Section 3.3 says it conditions on the full trajectory and averages the probability of “Yes” over stochastic reasoning rounds, but the supplied prompt contains only the question, external knowledge, and proposed solution, with no schema, observations, or requested reasoning. Appendix C describes paired positive/negative examples with randomized order even though the stated training task independently classifies one trajectory. It also says ground-truth SQL is inserted to help generate trajectories, despite this being the validator-data procedure.

Several methodology details are undefined or missing. The grounding reward omits cases such as predicting an irrelevant table when the gold label is relevant. Essential GRPO settings, sampling/group details, execution-equivalence implementation, random seeds, and uncertainty across runs are absent. The manuscript says “Code is available at” but provides no URL, code, or checkpoint. Filtering the training set using Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-4o is also not documented sufficiently to reproduce.

Originality is limited and overstated. Schema pruning, ReAct-style database interaction, execution-reward RL, best-of-N generation, and generative verification are all established ingredients. The paper's novelty is primarily their integration. More seriously, it adapts SkyRL-SQL—whose cited title explicitly concerns multi-turn RL for Text-to-SQL—without a direct experimental comparison, making claims such as the “first” interactive RL framework insufficiently supported.

The qualitative evidence contains conspicuous errors. Figure 6 presents thoughts, actions, and observations out of order: the agent discusses an empty result immediately after an OperationalError and later claims to fix the table name after already using the corrected name. Another case simply assumes that enrollment value 1.0 is a missing-value placeholder without database evidence, illustrating potentially harmful self-correction rather than semantic reliability.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on single-database execution accuracy, which can reward semantically incorrect queries that happen to return the same result. There is no test-suite accuracy, robustness analysis across database instances, statistical uncertainty, or convincing comparison under genuinely matched training and inference resources. The weak single-model multitask baselines are SFT-trained rather than given the same RL recipe, so they do not demonstrate that role specialization rather than training method causes the gain.

Limitations and ethics are incomplete. The paper discusses compute cost but not benchmark contamination, execution-accuracy false positives, dependence on access to database contents, or failure under schema/data shift. Its impact statement claims greater dependability while omitting important deployment risks from executing model-generated SQL, including unauthorized reads or writes, sensitive-data exposure, and expensive or adversarial queries. Sandboxing, read-only permissions, and human approval mechanisms are not specified.

Presentation quality is below the standard expected for acceptance: there are frequent typographical and grammatical errors, conflicting table values, an empty code link, and overconfident language such as “state-of-the-art,” “exceptional generalization,” and “orders of magnitude better” based partly on an unsupported extrapolation that SFT would require 15 million examples and 3–4 months. Overall, the promising benchmark numbers are not supported by a sufficiently consistent and reproducible empirical record.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical study is unusually broad. MARS-SQL reaches 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev, 89.75% on Spider-test, and 78.13% on Spider-DK, with additional SParC results. Component ablations, best-of-N curves, interaction-turn experiments, grounding precision/recall, and selection comparisons consistently support the usefulness of the overall workflow.

The evidence indicates that improvements are not solely due to parameter count or inference time. The paper compares against a roughly 21B ensemble, larger 14B and 32B single-model variants, and self-consistency baselines under an approximately matched 22-second latency budget. The verifier also substantially improves over self-consistency on BIRD-dev.

Significance: Training an open-weight Text-to-SQL system to use database feedback is practically useful, and the reported cross-domain performance is strong. The explicit latency, token, VRAM, and adjustable accuracy-cost analyses make the contribution more informative for deployment than a single headline accuracy number.

Originality and presentation: Individual ingredients—ReAct interaction, GRPO, schema pruning, and generative verification—are established, but their trainable role-specialized integration is a meaningful workflow-level contribution. The main architecture is clearly explained, with prompts and qualitative trajectories that make the intended behavior understandable.

The authors candidly report that the deployed system has an approximately 21B total parameter footprint despite using 7B modules, and discuss its higher inference cost. This honest limitation should be credited rather than penalized.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet adequate for an Accept rating. The displayed code link is empty, and essential RL details are missing or inconsistent: the prose reports batch size 64 while Table 4 reports 128; GRPO group size, KL coefficient, clipping coefficient, optimizer, token limits, advantage normalization, stopping behavior, and several decoding settings are not fully specified. The grounding reward definition also omits some non-exact prediction cases.

Several quantitative claims need reconciliation. The manuscript alternately describes approximately 35k labeled examples, 90,102 grounding instances, and approximately 16k verifier instances without clearly accounting for the generator data. GPT-5's Spider score differs between the main table and appendix, and generator-only/BIRD baseline values vary across tables without a sufficiently explicit mapping between configurations.

The causal interpretation of the controlled-isolation experiment is unclear. The three reported gains add exactly to the full improvement, but the text says each mechanism is added from a strict baseline; independent additions generally are not additive because schema pruning, interaction, sampling, and verification can interact. Exact configurations and evaluation randomness should be reported for every row.

The evaluation reports no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance analysis despite stochastic generation and verification. Consequently, very small differences—such as 89.75 versus 89.65 on Spider—do not substantiate a definitive state-of-the-art claim. Comparisons also mix systems with different model access, prompts, training data, and test-time budgets.

The qualitative evidence is imperfectly curated. Figure 6 orders the displayed thoughts and observations inconsistently—the text claims the table-name correction precedes the empty-result diagnosis, while the rendered trajectory places them differently—and includes malformed quoting. This weakens confidence in claims that these traces faithfully demonstrate learned self-correction.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: the central techniques are adaptations of prior multi-turn RL, ReAct, schema linking, best-of-N generation, and next-token generative verification. The paper should more sharply isolate its advance over SkyRL-SQL and other interactive Text-to-SQL RL systems instead of emphasizing broad 'first' or 'unique' language.

The limitations and ethics treatment focuses mainly on compute. A database-executing agent raises additional concerns—read-only sandboxing, destructive or injected SQL, sensitive-data exposure through observations, access control, benchmark-equivalent execution versus semantic correctness, and human oversight—which should be discussed before claiming dependable real-world or enterprise use.
